name: Castor oil eye drops

lead: Placing castor oil in the eyes is a folk practice sometimes said to soothe, clear or brighten them. It is distinct from regulated ophthalmic lubricant products, which are formulated and sterile.
The sources reviewed describe castor oil as an industrial and traditional-medicine oil and contain no information on its use as eye drops.

paras: Believers describe a lubricating or soothing effect. Castor oil is mostly ricinoleate fatty acids; the sources reviewed describe no tested mechanism for eye appearance.

Unformulated oil is not a sterile ophthalmic product. Encyclopedic sources note castor oil is sometimes claimed to treat diseases without supporting evidence, and note its oral laxative effects; ocular safety of raw oil is not covered by sources reviewed.

lead: Castor oil eye drops is a folk practice in which oil pressed from the seeds of Ricinus communis is placed in the eyes, with claims of soothing or brightening them. No published study of unformulated castor oil for this purpose was found.

Castor oil is about 90% ricinoleate fatty acids. It is produced mainly for industrial uses, has long served as a laxative, appears in cosmetics, and is used as a vehicle for some injected hormones. Encyclopedic sources note that it is sometimes claimed to cure diseases without supporting evidence [1].

paras: The seeds are 40 to 60 percent oil. The seeds contain ricin, a toxic lectin deactivated by heating during oil extraction [1]. The oil has been used as a laxative since at least the Ebers Papyrus, though modern sources describe it as medically discouraged for simple constipation because it can cause violent diarrhoea [1].
